meaning: The vital essence, life force, or double of a person. Created at birth and surviving death.

mythology.lead: The Egyptian ka is the vital double, the life-force that makes a person alive and that continues after death. Born with the body, shaped by the creator god, and sustained by offerings, the ka links the living, the dead, and the divine — existence understood as a maintained relationship, not a possession.

myths.title: The Ka Created at Birth
myths.text: Egyptian texts make the ka a companion formed together with the body itself. In the divine-birth scenes at Deir el-Bahari and Luxor, the ram-headed Khnum fashions the royal child and its ka on the potter's wheel while the frog-headed Heket breathes life into the finished form. The idea is far older than these New Kingdom reliefs: Pyramid Texts utterances already promise the king that his ka will stand at his side among the gods (Pyramid Texts, Utterance 213), and Coffin Texts Spell 80 bears the title 'for making the ka live'. To have a ka is simply to be alive — the word glosses 'vital essence, double, sustenance' — yet the ka is also a relationship: it belongs to the person, but it is made by a god, must be fed by a family, and will be judged among the dead. Egyptian anthropology never imagined life as a closed possession; it was a gift kept in circulation from the wheel of Khnum to the offering table of the tomb.

myths.title: The Ka After Death
myths.text: Death divides the person but does not dismiss the ka. The vital force leaves the corpse yet remains bound to it, returning to the mummy or to a statue made in the deceased's likeness — which is why every fine tomb of the Old Kingdom sets a reserve head or ka-statue in the serdab, a sealed chamber with an eye-slot through which the image could watch the sun rise and the offerings arrive. The rite that made this habitation lawful was the Opening of the Mouth, performed before mummy and statue alike: the adze touched the lips, and the ka could again receive breath, water, and bread. Letters to the dead from the Middle Kingdom — the Heqanakht correspondence — address the dead as powers who can be petitioned, reproached, and offended. The tomb chapel, the false door, the offering slab: all are engineering for a single need, that the ka never be cut off from its maintenance, because an unfed ka is not a soul in torment but a creditor at the door.

myths.title: The Ka and the Gods
myths.text: Kings possess not one ka but many: the royal titulary itself is ka-stuff, and the Horus-name lives as the king's divine double on earth, while Pyramid Texts utterances multiply the king's kas before Atum and the Ennead. The gods keep kas as well — 'Amun, his ka' is a standing formula of the Theban theology, and the ka of Ptah is invoked across the Memphite tradition. This is the ka's deepest office: it is the theological machinery of presence. A god is not in one place but in every temple that houses his image; not one being but as many as the names and cult statues that carry him. Long before later theologies wrestled with how the infinite can be present in many places, Egypt solved the problem practically — by giving power a double, and the double as many houses as piety could build. The ka is therefore not only personal but constitutional: the device by which authority becomes habitable.

myths.title: Feeding the Ka
myths.text: Every Egyptian offering invokes the ka by name. The formula ḥtp-di-nsw — 'an offering which the king gives' — routes bread, beer, oxen, and fowl through the king's generosity to the ka of god or dead, so that temple cult and tomb cult run on the same sentence. Book of the Dead Spell 105, 'for satisfying the ka in the necropolis', turns the meal into a speech-act with teeth: the ka swears it will not seize what is unlawful nor touch the offerings of another dead. Spell 110 admits the deceased to the Field of Iaru, where the ka eats of a harvest that grows cubits tall and the reaping is easy. The Egyptians understood with a clarity modern religion rarely matches that the dead are dependents — that survival is a budget. A society is measured, the spells imply, not by the height of its pyramids but by how faithfully it feeds what it claims to honor, year after year, when the feeding has stopped being spectacular.

phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k], the initial consonant of the life-force.
Long open vowel [aː], inferred from Coptic and from the word's prosodic weight.
Final Egyptological aleph [ʔ], a glottal catch that leaves the root open like a breath.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAH-ah' — say a firm ka, hold the vowel, then close with a soft glottal catch.

pronunciation.note: The ka is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves the final Egyptological aleph (ꜣ) — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Egyptian vowels are not written in hieroglyphs and must be reconstructed.

domains.title: The Vital Double
domains.subtitle: Life-Force · Sustenance · Divine Presence
domains.lead: The Egyptian kꜣ is the life-force that makes a person alive, the vital double created at birth and sustained by offerings. Where the ba is the mobile personality, the ka remains tethered to the body and the tomb, consuming the spiritual essence of bread, beer, and meat.

cards.name: Created at Birth
cards.desc: Khnum shapes the infant and its ka on the potter's wheel; Heket breathes life into the finished form.

cards.name: Sustained by Offerings
cards.desc: Tombs are 'houses of the ka'; the formula 'an offering which the king gives' feeds it after death.

cards.name: Statue Body
cards.desc: A ka-statue in the serdab provides a form for the ka if the body perishes, its eyes on the sun.

cards.name: Divine Ka
cards.desc: Kings possess multiple kas; gods extend their presence into every temple through ka-doubles.

lore.syncretism:
The ka has no direct counterpart in Greek or Roman religion, but related ideas circulated.

Greek authors sometimes interpreted Egyptian ka-statues as 'doubles' or 'guardian spirits,' and the Roman genius and Juno concepts may have faintly echoed the idea of a personal life-force. In Coptic Christianity, the old vocabulary of ka and ba was largely replaced by Greek pneuma and psychē, though the practice of offering food at tombs survived in modified forms. Modern Theosophy and Hermeticism revived the ka as the 'etheric double,' an energetic body that sustains the physical form. In Kemetic reconstruction, the ka remains a central concept: the life-force that must be fed, remembered, and honored.
lore.culturalLegacy:
The ka survives wherever people speak of a life-force or energy body.

From Theosophical 'etheric doubles' to New Age 'auras,' from Chinese qi to Hindu prāṇa, modern seekers have repeatedly rediscovered the Egyptian intuition that physical life depends on an invisible sustaining power. The ka's need for offerings has been reinterpreted as the need for attention, memory, and ritual care. In museums, ka-statues stand as reminders that the Egyptians imagined survival as a social act: the dead continue only if the living continue to feed them. The ka is thus ancestor to every modern practice that treats the dead as ongoing participants in family life.
lore.extendedMeditation: The Egyptian ka quietly contradicts every modern theory of the self. It is not the body, since it can abandon the corpse and inhabit a statue; not the personality, since that office belongs to the ba, the bird that comes and goes; not the soul in the Christian sense, since a ka can be hungry, offended, and fed with bread. The ka is the simple and radical claim that to be alive is to be accompanied — that a person is not a closed unit but an open circuit requiring sustenance, attention, and a dwelling. The tomb stelae that beg passers-by to speak the dead's name, the offering tables renewed at festivals, the ka-statue standing in the serdab with a slot for the gaze: all are engineering for this maintenance. To read the ka rightly is to see why the Egyptians feared the nameless dead more than the dangerous ones, and why their deepest prayer was so modest — that the ka be satisfied, and the name continue.
lore.archaeology: Ka-statues and offering chapels dominate the archaeological record. The reserve heads of the Fourth Dynasty from Giza and the wooden statue of the official Kaaper (Fifth Dynasty, Saqqara; the so-called 'Sheikh el-Beled' companion) provided alternative bodies for the ka, while the many ka-statues of officials from Saqqara and Giza filled their serdabs. Offering tables and false doors in the tomb chapels of Thebes and Memphis — the mastabas of Ti and Mereruka preserve whole processions of offering-bearers approaching the tomb owner's ka — directed food to the life-force. Middle Kingdom letters to the dead (the Heqanakht archive) show the cult operating in real families, and the New Kingdom divine-birth colonnades at Deir el-Bahari carve Khnum at his wheel in stone.
